news.title: GE Vernova, Hitachi, SGE and Samsung C&T sign BWRX-300s MoU

scraped_data.text:
The signatories of the memorandum of understanding - Poland's SGE, the US's GE Vernova, Japan's Hitachi and South Korea's Samsung C&T - will establish "a framework for cooperation on market development and commercial opportunities" for the deployment of the BWRX-300 small modular reactor (SMR).
GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy, a joint venture between GE Vernova and Hitachi, is the designer of the BWRX-300. Samsung Construction and Trading Corporation (Samsung C&T) has considerable experience in major nuclear and energy infrastructure projects. SGE is already developing projects for a fleet of BWRX-300 reactors in Europe, notably in Poland and the UK.
The official announcement of the MOU signing said it was "linked to the memorandum of cooperation for SMR deployment in third countries signed on the margins of this year's NATO summit by United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Japan Foreign Minister Motegi Toshimitsu, and Republic of Korea Foreign Minister Cho Hyun".
It said the US Department of State saw it as "a concrete industry effort to advance BWRX-300 deployment across Europe and deepen government-industry cooperation on global energy security".
In quotes
Roger Martella, GE Vernova's Chief Corporate Officer and Chief Sustainability Officer, said: "GE Vernova has a long-standing history and presence across the European continent. This collaboration brings together complementary capabilities to help advance BWRX-300 deployment across multiple markets and build on the momentum already behind the technology."
Yasunori Inada, CEO of Nuclear Energy Business Unit, Hitachi, said: "This collaboration brings together the strengths and expertise of each partner, and Hitachi will contribute to exploring the deployment of the BWRX-300 in Europe by drawing on the technological capabilities cultivated through our nuclear business and on our collaboration with qualified Japanese suppliers."
Jung Wook Kim, Executive Vice President and Head of Global Business Unit and Global Operation, Samsung C&T, said: "Samsung C&T is honoured to open a new chapter in Europe's SMR business together with GE Vernova, Hitachi and SGE. Building on Samsung C&T's proven EPC capabilities, we will fully leverage the synergy created by this four-way partnership to strengthen Europe's energy security and contribute to the realisation of carbon neutrality."
Michał Sołowow, founder of SGE, said: "Europe and the UK need a scalable commercial model for new nuclear, built on proven technology, established supply chains and world-class delivery partners. By combining GE Vernova Hitachi's BWRX-300 technology, Hitachi's industrial capabilities and Samsung C&T's global construction expertise, SGE is creating a platform to deploy standardised nuclear fleets across multiple markets."
Background
The BWRX-300 is a 300 MWe water-cooled, natural circulation SMR with passive safety systems that leverages the design and licensing basis of GVH's US Nuclear Regulatory Commission-certified ESBWR boiling water reactor design and its existing, licensed GNF2 fuel design, a unique combination that GVH says positions it to deliver an "innovative, carbon-free baseload power generation source" this decade.
The first BWRX-300 is under construction at Ontario Power Generation's Darlington site in Canada, with completion expected by the end of the decade.
SGE has a number of potential projects under way across Europe - including in Poland, where a decision in principle has been issued for 26 BWRX-300 SMRs, and in the UK where a proposal for a fleet of 14 of the SMRs across three sites is being considered under the UK’s Advanced Nuclear Framework programme.

news.title: Škoda JS to supply control rod drives for Rolls-Royce SMR's reactors

scraped_data.text:
Škoda JS is part of the Czech majority state-owned CEZ Group, which also has a 20% stake in UK-based Rolls-Royce SMR.
Earlier this year Škoda JS and Doosan Enerbility were selected by Rolls-Royce SMR for pre-production work for key components - including the reactor pressure vessel - with work which encompasses "early supplier engagement, design finalisation and manufacturing readiness to support the delivery of first power at the earliest possible date".
The Pilsen-based firm has now added the contract for the control rod drive mechanisms, which are key bits of equipment in a nuclear reactor, ensuring the precise movement of the control rods which control the reactor’s power, ensuring its safe operation. According to CEZ "each drive is a unique electromechanical linear motor, almost eight metres long and weighing 450 kg, capable of safely controlling the nuclear reactor in all operating modes".
Czech Minister of Industry and Trade Karel Havlíček said: "Small modular reactors are a technological opportunity for our companies with global reach. The contracts that Škoda JS has already concluded with Rolls-Royce SMR are clear proof of this. Small modular reactors will not only strengthen the energy security and self-sufficiency of our country, but will also create new jobs and create opportunities for follow-up investments."
The first of Rolls-Royce SMR's 470 MWe small modular reactors is due to be built in North Wales in the UK, with the first in the Czech Republic to be built at Temelín, with an expected operational date "in the second half of the 2030s" and with five or six more units to follow across three sites.
Rolls-Royce SMR CEO Chris Cholerton said: "Škoda JS has proven that it is one of the few companies in Europe capable of providing one of the most important components of our power plant … our cooperation shows the clear benefits that this project brings to industrial companies."
Daniel Beneš, Chairman and CEO of ČEZ, said: "A global supply chain for small modular reactors is now being formed, and it is essential for our industrial companies to act quickly and now. This opportunity is unique. If they manage to get involved in this chain right from the start, they can win attractive contracts for the next decades. Škoda JS now faces the task of developing a prototype directly for small modular reactors so that it can subsequently supply them to Rolls-Royce SMR all over the world."
Background
The Rolls-Royce SMR is a 470 MWe design based on a small pressurised water reactor. It will provide consistent baseload generation for at least 60 years. Ninety percent of the SMR - measuring about 16 metres by 4 metres - will be built in factory conditions, limiting activity on-site primarily to assembly of pre-fabricated, pre-tested, modules which significantly reduces project risk and has the potential to drastically shorten build schedules.
In October 2024, Rolls-Royce SMR was selected by ČEZ to deploy up to 3 GW of electricity in the Czech Republic, and ČEZ took a 20% stake in Rolls-Royce SMR. The plan is for the first SMR to be deployed in the area of the Temelín site (which already has two gigawatt-scale VVER-1000 units), with further projects being developed for coal-fired power plant sites, including Tušimice.
In June 2025, Rolls-Royce SMR was selected as the UK government's preferred technology for the country's first SMR project. In November, the UK government announced that Wylfa on the island of Anglesey, North Wales, would be the site to host the three Rolls-Royce SMR units. It said the site - where a Magnox plant is being decommissioned - could potentially host up to eight SMRs. A final investment decision is expected to be taken in 2029.
Škoda JS has long experience in the construction and servicing of nuclear power plants, including manufacturing 21 VVER-440 reactors and three VVER-1000 reactors, as well as supplying engineering, equipment and servicing for nuclear power plants, research reactors and spent nuclear fuel storage facilities in Central and Eastern Europe, Scandinavia, France, Germany, the USA, Austria, Finland, Belgium, the UK, China and Armenia.

news.title: SGE confident of UK SMR fleet prospects

scraped_data.text:
SGE (formerly Synthos Green Energy) in July submitted an application under the UK's Advanced Nuclear Framework for reactors which could provide 4.2 GW of capacity, equivalent to 11% of current UK power demand.
Poland's SGE - whose deployment team includes Samsung C&T, Laing O'Rourke, Aecon Group and Google Cloud - says it will privately finance the deployment of the fleet of GE Vernova Hitachi’s BWRX-300 small modular reactors (SMRs) across three sites in the UK.
The plan is for the initial site to host six of the 300 MW SMRs, with four each at two subsequent sites. The locations of the proposed sites have not yet been disclosed, pending final negotiations.
Rafał Kasprów, CEO of SGE, told World Nuclear News, "I think the UK market has amazing opportunities for SMR developers, and especially us with a fleet approach".
From the financial point of view he says "we are bringing this investment to the UK … with the disruptive model of not asking government to cover everything on the development and construction phase. We are asking the UK government for Contract for Differences for a fleet of reactors. So it is only when electrons are delivered to the grid that we can benefit from the Contract for Difference model".
The Contract for Difference (CfD) would work by a future price being agreed for electricity generated by the SMRs - if the price of electricity is higher, the developer will pay the extra back, and if the price of electricity is below the agreed level, the difference is provided to the developer. In the energy sector, a CfD acts as a very long-term price stabilisation mechanism. The UK used a Contract for Difference funding model for Hinkley Point C, but moved away from it for the Sizewell C project.
SGE's project is currently going through the "deep dive" stage of the UK's Advanced Nuclear Framework which they believe will conclude in October or November and allow them to be part of the pipeline, and start to execute the project.
As an investor in the project, SGE says that it knows what it needs to do internally to de-risk the project "so we know how to translate that same conversation to markets".
Kasprów, seated, centre, at June's event outlining its UK fleet plan (Image: SGE)
The company has also developed plans for a fleet of SMRs in Poland and in June submitted its contract for difference application to the government there. As to which country's projects might happen first, Kasprów says that the UK project could happen at the same time, praising the UK regulatory regime and its infrastructure.
He also rejected concerns about the capacity of supply chains and workforce to cope with the construction of Sizewell C and a number of SMR projects at the same time. He stressed the maturity of the BWRX-300 technology, its use of existing nuclear fuels and the example and experience of the first unit being constructed in Canada.
"We are using existing supply chains - there is also an advantage to the fleet approach because there are places where the supply chain exists, but maybe needs to scale up, and by coming to market with a 14-unit project as our starting point those companies can see a clear path to making that investment worthwhile," said Robert Rudich, Chief Business Development Manager.
They also stress that the non-nuclear part of the plant is similar to conventional power plants, with the industrial giants GE Vernova and Hitachi as partners and all part of a Europe-wide supply chain.
GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy's BWRX-300 is a 300 MWe water-cooled, natural circulation SMR with passive safety systems that leverages the design and licensing basis of the company's US Nuclear Regulatory Commission-certified ESBWR boiling water reactor design and its existing, licensed GNF2 fuel design, a unique combination that GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy says positions it to deliver an "innovative, carbon-free baseload power generation source" this decade.
The first BWRX-300 is under construction at Ontario Power Generation's Darlington site in Canada, with completion expected by the end of the decade. The Darlington project is a reference project for OSGE.
Luba Kotzeva, founder and CEO of advisory and consultancy group Etara and part of the project team, said there had been "good engagement" with the UK side on the issue of a Contract for Difference funding model and stressed the importance of the proposal being for a fleet programme: "I think that is essential to getting the economies of scale, to getting the economics to flow, to getting the private capital."
The example of the first SMR being built in a G7 country, at Darlington in Canada, is also seen as a key development. Kasprów said: "It's extremely important, it is the difference between having something and nothing. It's not about promises anymore - it's happening."

news.title: Second reactor manufactured for floating nuclear plant

scraped_data.text:
The floating nuclear power plant, FPU-106, will feature two of the 58 MWe RITM-200C reactors - the first was manufactured in May and is at the shipyard awaiting installation. The units have been manufactured at Rosatom's Mechanical Engineering Division’s ZiO-Podolsk plant.
Anton Lebedev, head of ZiO-Podolsk, said: "2026 has been a landmark year for ZiO-Podolsk's mechanical engineering teams: for the first time, we have produced a complete set of RITM units for a floating nuclear power plant that will supply power to an industrial cluster in the Russian North. This is an important step in the global development of small modular nuclear power. The plant has also set a record this year: in less than a year, four RITM-family units have already been manufactured, with five more in production."
The RITM-200C is an adapted version of the RITM-200 reactors used on Russia's nuclear icebreaker fleet.
In total, the Baimskaya development requires around 300 MWe, therefore, three such 100+ MWe floating power plants are needed, while a fourth will be installed as backup for outages during refuelling and maintenance.
In total, 16 RITM units have been produced. Eight are in operation on the nuclear icebreakers Arktika, Ural, Sibir, and Yakutia. A further 12 units are at various stages of manufacturing.
Rosatom says that when complete, the Chukotka project "will be the world's first green energy project for industrial production based on a floating power unit".
Russia has the world's only operating floating nuclear power plant, the Akademik Lomonosov which began commercial operation in May 2020. It is based, with its coastal infrastructure, by the city of Pevek - population 5,000 - to which it supplies heat and power in Russia's Arctic Chukotka region.
The Akademik Lomonosov has two KLT-40S reactors generating 35 MWe each, which are similar to those used in a previous generation of nuclear-powered icebreakers. It has the capacity to provide electricity to a city with a population of up to 100,000 people.
As well as the four floating power units under construction, Rosatom is targeting the export market for floating nuclear power plants.

news.title: US-Turkey agreement to accelerate SMR deployment

scraped_data.text:
Last November, Turkey's energy minister set out a target to deploy 5000 MWe of small modular reactor (SMR) capacity - in addition to 12 larger reactors - by 2050. The US Trade and Development Agency's (USTDA) assistance will identify the policy and investment steps needed to bring SMRs to market, producing recommendations to TÜNAŞ that Turkey's Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources and the Turkish Nuclear Regulatory Authority can then use to establish a clear, workable framework for SMR deployment through updates to the country's nuclear regulations and procedures, USTDA said.
The work will also include a review of how US reactor designs could meet Turkey's needs, which USTDA said will give US SMR companies an early entry point into Turkey's civil nuclear sector.
According to Turkey's Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources, the year-long study will evaluate SMR designs from four US companies, as well as five 4th generation US reactor designs, from technical, economic, regulatory and licensing perspectives, culminating in the preparation of technical reports. The agreement has a budget of around USD2 million, with USTDA covering the technical work.
"Our goal is to advance TÜNAŞ's efforts to create the conditions for deploying SMRs, which can increase energy security for Türkiye while providing opportunities for U.S. companies," USTDA Deputy Director Thomas Hardy said. "This framework will incorporate international expertise in this fast-moving field while tailoring it to Türkiye's specific needs."
The USTDA acts as the US government's "first mover" on critical infrastructure development in emerging markets, advancing shared priorities with partner countries while creating opportunities for deployment of US solutions. Amongst other things, it funds up-front technical work that accelerates the development of infrastructure projects, helping them attract the financing they need for implementation and procurement of US goods and services.
TÜNAŞ (Türkiye Nükleer Enerji Anonim Şirketi) is a subsidiary of Turkish state generating company Elektrik Üretim AŞ (EÜAŞ) and was established in 2022 to carry out the construction, operation, maintenance, and repair of nuclear power plants in Turkey.
The agreement was signed in New York by Hardy and TÜNAŞ General Manager Necati Yamaç in the presence of Turkey's Energy and Natural Resources Minister Alparslan Bayraktar, who said: "In line with our 2053 Net Zero Emissions and full energy independence goals, we are determined to diversify our energy mix. In addition to our large-scale nuclear power plants, we will resolutely continue to build a strong and modern energy infrastructure by meticulously studying the most suitable alternatives for our country's needs."
Turkey's first nuclear power plant, comprising four Russian-designed VVER-1200 reactors, is under construction at Akkuyu in the southern Mersin province. It is being built by Russia's Rosatom under a so-called BOO (build-own-operate) model. TÜNAŞ has previously signed memorandums of understanding on nuclear cooperation covering project development, technology transfer, site evaluation and financing with Korea Electric Power Corporation and Canada's Candu Energy, part of AtkinsRéalis.

news.title: Polish plant contract negotiations move to next stage

scraped_data.text:
The terms and conditions that have now been agreed provide a framework for the negotiation of further specific elements of the contract and its exhibits and to finalise the remaining terms by year-end, the three companies said. ('Exhibits' are various supplementary documents to a contract that provide additional details, specifications or other supporting information).
In November 2022, the then Polish government selected Westinghouse AP1000 reactor technology for construction at the Lubiatowo-Kopalino site in the Choczewo municipality in Pomerania in northern Poland. In September 2023, Westinghouse, Bechtel and Polskie Elektrownie Jądrowe (PEJ) - a special-purpose vehicle 100% owned by Poland's State Treasury - signed an 18-month engineering services contract for Westinghouse and Bechtel will finalise a site-specific design for the plant.
"With this agreement, we continue our close partnership with PEJ for the delivery of our proven, advanced AP1000 reactor for this historic project," said Dan Lipman, President of Global Business Initiatives at Westinghouse. "The proven, advanced AP1000 reactor will provide Poland with abundant, reliable energy, contribute billions of zlotys to its economy and create thousands of jobs in both countries during construction and operation."
The second phase of preparatory works and in-depth geological surveys are already being conducted at the future construction site, with general contractor Bechtel assuming management of the project site in August, as earthworks began. PEJ submitted a construction licence application to Poland's National Atomic Energy Agency in March.
PEJ's 'behind the scenes' video of site works (Video: PEJ)
Dena Volovar, President of Bechtel's Nuclear, Security & Environmental business, said the latest agreement reflects the momentum the company has built with PEJ and is a "vote of confidence in American nuclear technology and know-how".
"Bechtel has designed, built, or supported 150 nuclear power plants over 80 years, and we recently completed the most modern AP1000 units in the United States. Using modern execution tools to drive efficient delivery, we're bringing that experience to Poland, and we're building local capability as we go. By the time this plant is running, Polish companies and Polish workers will be part of a nuclear industry that can compete for decades," he said.
"PEJ and the Westinghouse-Bechtel consortium have agreed on the main terms of the contract for the construction of the first Polish nuclear power plant, which provides the basis for further, detailed negotiations regarding the remaining terms of cooperation under the EPC Contract," said Marek Woszczyk, President of Polskie Elektrownie Jadrowe. "The American Westinghouse-Bechtel consortium will be responsible for the construction of the facility, with the first electricity to the Polish grid from the power plant to flow in 2036."

news.title: First concrete poured for Bailong 2 nuclear power unit

scraped_data.text:
The landmark moment at the State Power Investment Corporation site, in the Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region of southern China, means two units are now officially under construction.
According to the report on China's CCTV television channel, carried on State Power Investment Corporation's Weibo channel, the initial concrete pour was expected to be 6,637 cubic metres over 58 hours.
The construction of Phase I (units 1 and 2) of the Bailong plant was among approvals for 11 new reactors granted by China's State Council in August 2024. State Power Investment Corporation plans to build two CAP1000 pressurised water reactors - the Chinese version of the Westinghouse AP1000 - as the first phase of the plant. An investment of about CNY40 billion (USD5.6 billion) is planned for the two units, which are expected to take 56 months to construct.
Excavation work for the foundation pit of the nuclear island for unit 1 began in late December 2024. SPIC subsidiary Shanghai Nuclear Engineering Research & Design Institute (SNERDI) - joint general contractor for the project - announced it poured the first concrete for that unit on 22 December 2025. The company said a total of 6,662 cubic metres of concrete was poured in a process lasting just over 64 hours.
Located on Jiangshan Peninsula in Fangchenggang City, Guangxi Province, the Bailong plant is planned to have six units, with a total installed capacity of 8.62 GWe and a total investment of approximately CNY120 billion. The first phase of the project adopts the CAP1000 design, with each unit having a capacity of 1.25 GW. Four larger CAP1400 reactors are also proposed to be built at the site - located about 24 kilometres from the border with Vietnam and about 30 kilometres southwest of China General Nuclear's Fangchenggang nuclear power plant - in later phases.
After the first phase of the project is completed and put into operation, it is expected to generate about 20 billion kilowatt-hours of electricity per year, which is equivalent to reducing standard coal consumption by about 6 million tonnes and carbon dioxide emissions by about 16 million tonnes per year.

news.title: Tianwan 7 brought to minimum controllable power level

scraped_data.text:
Nuclear fuel was loaded into the reactor core in August and specialists will now conduct a series of tests and checks before the power level can be increased. Such checks and tests will continue as power is increased in stages before getting to full power as part of the commissioning process.
Alexey Likhachev, Director General of the Rosatom, which is building the unit in China, said: "The Tianwan Nuclear Power Plant is a model project for our collaboration with China. Units 1 and 2, built to our design, have been operating here for two decades now. It will soon be 10 years since the launch of Units 3 and 4, and today we are reaching a key milestone in the launch of the new units.
"Our collaboration with Chinese nuclear scientists demonstrates the highest level of coordination and efficiency: construction of Units 7 and 8 began just over five years ago, and today, one could say, the heart of the reactor at Unit 7 has begun beating. This is a great success and an excellent result of our collaboration."
The background
In June 2018, Russia and China signed agreements for the construction of two VVER-1200 reactors as units 7 and 8 of the Tianwan plant. Construction of unit 7 began in May 2021, with that of unit 8 starting in February 2022. The units have been scheduled to be put into commercial operation in 2026 and 2027, respectively.
The Tianwan nuclear power plant is owned and operated by Jiangsu Nuclear Power Company, a joint venture between China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC) (50%), China Power Investment Corporation (30%) and Jiangsu Guoxin Group (20%).
The first four units at the Tianwan site - which began commercial operation between June 2007 and December 2018 - are Gidropress VVER units supplied by Russia. Units 5 and 6 both feature Chinese ACPR1000 reactors.
In January, CNNC announced that hot tests - which simulate the temperatures and pressures the reactor systems will be subjected to during normal operation - had been completed at unit 7 on 30 December. Cold tests - which verify the leak-tightness of the primary circuit and components - were completed at unit 8 earlier this month.
Once all units at the Tianwan plant are operational, the total installed capacity will exceed 9 GWe, with an annual power generation of over 70 TWh, reducing carbon dioxide emissions by 57.4 million tonnes annually.

news.title: Armenia to make new nuclear decision 'in near future'

scraped_data.text:
According to the Prime Minister's official report on the meeting, the two sides "discussed issues related to the work on extending the operating life of the second power unit of the Armenian NPP and the proposals of the Russian side on the construction of a new nuclear power unit in our country".
Russia's state nuclear corporation's in-house publication Strana Rosatom reported that Likhachev said that most of the work planned for the period up to 2031 relating to the life extension to 2036 has already been completed.
It added that "the Armenian side is also exploring the possibility of further extending the unit's operation - from 2036 to 2046".
According to the head of Rosatom, it reported, "this is technically feasible, but will require significant investment in upgrading safety and automation systems, re-annealing the reactor vessel, and expanding and repairing spent nuclear fuel storage facilities. The investment could reach hundreds of millions of dollars".
New nuclear capacity
Armenia's prime minister said the government was in discussions about "proposals received from international partners on the construction of a new nuclear power unit and a decision will be made in the near future" and he "emphasised that the final decision will be of an exclusively economic nature, taking into account the price, quality, safety, deadlines and guarantees".
The prime minister's official account of the meeting added that Likhachev "presented details on the proposals and possible mechanisms for the construction of a new NPP, as well as small and medium-capacity power units".
According to Strana Rosatom, Likhachev explained: "We made a specific proposal to the Armenian government for a 1,000-watt unit based on our flagship VVER-1000 design. These are the VVERs we are replicating domestically; these are the VVERs we built and continue to build in India and Iran. They combine extremely high economic efficiency, namely low electricity costs, with all the necessary Generation III+ safety systems."
Background
Armenia currently operates one nuclear reactor - a 376 MWe VVER reactor at the Armenia Nuclear Power plant, which started operating in 1980. The plant was home to two units, which were taken offline in 1988 due to safety concerns regarding seismic vulnerability. Unit 2 was restarted in 1995, and Rosatom is currently collaborating in a project to extend the unit's life to 2036. Unit 1 is now being decommissioned.
Armenia has been considering the potential construction of new nuclear capacity for some time. In January 2022, Rosatom and the management of the Armenian Nuclear Power Plant signed an agreement to look into the possible building of new Russian-designed nuclear power units on the site of the current plant at Metsamor.
Earlier this year Armenia's Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure David Khudatyan, speaking at a press conference, said Armenia was reviewing proposed "modular nuclear reactor" models from Russia, the USA, France, China, and South Korea, according to the Armenpress news agency.
In February Pashinyan and US Vice President JD Vance signed a joint statement on the completion of negotiations on the Agreement on Cooperation between the Government of the Republic of Armenia and the Government of the United States of America in the Field of Peaceful Use of Nuclear Energy during Vance's visit to Armenia. That agreement would enable US and Armenian companies to "strike deals" on civil nuclear projects, Vance said.

news.title: First construction permit issued for BWRX-300 SMR in the US

scraped_data.text:
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) said its decision "paves the way for the nation's first commercial small modular reactor". It said it completed the review in 14 months, four months earlier than it had scheduled.
NRC Chairman Ho Nieh said: "Today's Clinch River decision demonstrates that the new NRC can make rigorous and credible safety decisions that enable major American nuclear projects to move forward."
Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA), which is a government-owned power company, said that although no construction date has been announced, it is now the first US utility permitted to construct the BWRX‑300 small modular reactor (SMR). It said it "continues negotiations with industry partners to ensure responsible cost sharing and financial accountability throughout design and construction".
Mike Skaggs, TVA Interim President and CEO, said: "This construction permit is more than a regulatory achievement, it's foundational for America's nuclear future." TVA's Chief Nuclear Officer Matt Rasmussen said: "The NRC's strong engagement with the industry is essential to support America's energy leadership and help build the foundation for the nation's advanced nuclear future."
TVA said that the Clinch River permit "establishes a clear, repeatable licensing pathway for future BWRX-300 SMR applicants, improving predictability, lowering barriers, and accelerating deployment timelines nationwide." And Skaggs added that the priority now was "ensuring the people of the Valley do not shoulder the costs of first‑of‑a‑kind technology that benefits the nation and world. Strategic partnerships enable shared responsibility, shared value, and shared progress as we deploy advanced nuclear infrastructure to meet our nation’s energy security and AI dominance goals".
Mike Skaggs, left, and Jeremy Bowen from the NRC (Image: GE Vernova Hitachi)
Eric Gray, CEO of GE Vernova Power Segment, said: "This is a milestone for TVA and GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy, and an important moment for new nuclear in the United States. TVA has shown strong leadership in advancing new nuclear, a commitment bolstered by the collaborative efforts of the NRC and Department of Energy. Together, and in alignment with federal Executive Orders aimed at accelerating advanced reactors, we are grateful for this collaboration as we work to support the deployment of the first BWRX-300 in the country."
Jason Cooper, CEO of GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy, said: "Fleet deployment is essential to scaling nuclear energy in the United States. A standard design, combined with a predictable and efficient regulatory environment, allows us to apply common technology, licensing experience, supply chain capabilities and lessons learned from one project to the next. Clinch River brings us another step closer to making that fleet model a reality."
State Governor Bill Lee said: "The Clinch River project represents the next chapter in our state's legacy of innovation, strengthening America's energy security and creating opportunity for generations to come."
The NRC formally began its review in July 2025. It included a safety evaluation completed by the NRC staff in June, which found that TVA's construction permit application met all regulatory requirements. The NRC also held a public hearing in Oak Ridge, Tennessee, in August.
The background
The Tennessee Valley Authority submitted its application for Clinch River to the NRC in May 2025, making it the first utility in the USA to submit a construction permit application for GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy's BWRX-300 technology.
Small modular reactors - SMRs - are reactors with a smaller and more modular design than the USA's currently operating commercial nuclear fleet. As well as offering safety enhancements, their smaller footprint and modular design means they can potentially be built more quickly, are easier to operate and better fit into the landscape due to their compact size, TVA said.
TVA already holds an early site permit for SMRs at the Clinch River site, certifying that the site near Oak Ridge, Tennessee, is suitable for the construction of a nuclear power plant from the point of view of site safety, environmental impact and emergency planning. It has also completed and submitted an Environmental Report for the project to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
The BWRX-300 design is a 300 MWe water-cooled, natural circulation SMR with passive safety systems that leverages the design and licensing basis of the ESBWR boiling water reactor developed by GEH. The first BWRX-300 unit is currently under construction in Canada, the first of four of the SMRs planned at the Darlington New Nuclear Project site.
In September 2026, Blue Energy submitted the first part of its construction permit application to the NRC for a BWRX-300 planned for its gas-plus-nuclear project in Texas. There are also projects advancing for fleet deployment of BWRX-300 units in Poland and the UK.

news.title: Hinkley Point C completes 620-metre tunnel for fish

scraped_data.text:
According to EDF, the completion of the five month-long tunnelling project under the Bristol Channel means that, in total, more than eight kilometres of marine tunnels have been dug as part of the new nuclear power plant project.
The boring machine has now been picked up by a floating crane, and is being taken away for cleaning before being used on another site.
(Image: EDF)
Fish protection
Power stations on the coast use seawater in their cooling water systems and Hinkley Point C, in southwest England, is using "specially designed intake heads to slow the speed of water entering the cooling tunnels, allowing fish to escape from as close 2 metres in the 20-kilometre-wide channel". The intake tunnels are each 3.4 kilometres long with a diameter of six metres. There is also one outfall tunnel, 1.8 kilometres long with an internal diameter of seven metres.
An EDF graphic showing how the fish return system will work (Image: EDF)
In addition, there is also an innovative 'fish disco' system of underwater acoustics being planned to keep fish away from the water intake areas. Finally, there is the fish return system to transfer fish that do enter the system back to the sea. Taken together, EDF says that the GBP700 million (USD955 million) fish protection systems mean the new plant will have more fish protection measures than any other power plant in the world.
Background
Construction of Hinkley Point C - composed of two EPR pressurised water reactors of 1,630 MWe each - began in December 2018, with unit 1 of the plant originally scheduled to start up by the end of 2025, before that was revised to 2027 in May 2022. "This key milestone marks the completion of the civil engineering construction of the unit's inner containment structure, laying a solid foundation for subsequent prestressed containment construction and the installation of core nuclear equipment," it noted.
The HPR1000 (Hualong One) reactor design features a double-layered containment building, the main function of which is to ensure the integrity and leak tightness of the reactor building, and it plays a key role in the containment of radioactive substances.
China's Ministry of Ecology and Environment issued construction licences for Zhangzhou units 1 and 2 - both featuring Hualong One reactors - in October 2019 to CNNC-Guodian Zhangzhou Energy Company, the owner of the Zhangzhou nuclear power project, which was created by CNNC (51%) and China Guodian Corporation (49%) in 2011. Construction of Zhangzhou 1 began in October 2019, with that of unit 2 starting in September 2020. Unit 1 entered commercial operation on 1 January 2025 while unit 2 entered commercial operation on 1 January 2026.
In September 2022, China's State Council approved the construction of two further Hualong One units as Phase II - units 3 and 4 - of the Zhangzhou plant. Construction of unit 3 began in February 2024, with that of unit 4 starting in September. The inner steel safety dome was installed on the containment building of unit 3 in early February this year.
There are proposals for two more Hualong One units at the plant. Once fully completed, a six-unit Zhangzhou plant would provide more than 60 billion kilowatt-hours of clean energy annually, estimated to meet 75% of the total electricity consumption of Xiamen and Zhangzhou cities in southern Fujian.
Zhaoyuan concrete pours
Meanwhile, China General Nuclear (CGN) said the first phase (units 1 and 2) of the Zhaoyuan plant had entered its peak civil construction period. It said that concrete pouring for "the inner five layers and outer one layer" of the reactor building for unit 1 of the Zhaoyuan plant had been completed, while the construction of internal wall panels "is proceeding smoothly".
In addition, unit 2 had achieved the first concrete pour for the nuclear island, conventional island, and cooling tower. Offshore engineering and the construction of onshore water intake and drainage pipelines, CGN said, are also progressing steadily.
In November 2022, the Ministry of Ecology and Environment announced the formal acceptance of the environmental impact assessment documents covering the site selection stage for the Zhaoyuan plant. Construction of Phase I of the plant was approved by China's State Council in August 2024. First concrete was poured for unit 1 in November 2025, with that for unit 2 following on 5 September this year.
The plant, representing a total investment of about CNY120 billion (USD16.9 billion), will eventually house six Hualong One units. Each unit is expected to start generating power 50-60 months after the start of its construction. With a total installed capacity of 7.2 GWe, the plant is expected to generate 50 TWh of electricity annually - enough to meet the yearly needs of about five million people. It will be equivalent to cutting standard coal consumption by roughly 15.27 million tonnes and reducing carbon dioxide emissions by about 46.2 million tonnes each year, according to CGN.
The Zhaoyuan plant project marks the first application of secondary circulation large-scale seawater cooling systems at a nuclear power plant in China. Each unit will be equipped with a 203-metre-high high-level water-collecting natural draft cooling tower with a water-spraying area of 16,800 square metres, changing the direct cooling source of the conventional island of the nuclear power plant from the ocean to the atmosphere.

"Nuclear power is not a return to the past: it is a winning technology, which, when integrated with renewables, can deliver extraordinary results for our energy security, toward neutrality by 2050."
Addressing the Senate, he said: "The international climate has changed profoundly in recent years. Energy market volatility, geopolitical tensions, the need to reduce dependence on fossil fuels, and increasingly ambitious decarbonisation goals have highlighted the need for the government to simultaneously ensure environmental sustainability, energy security, and affordability for families and businesses.
In this context, the nuclear debate has taken on a new dimension compared to the past.
"The Government believes that Italy, in this unstable geopolitical context and with strong international competition, cannot stand idly by and watch developments taking place in other countries, which have always benefited from Italy's excellence in this sector. It is therefore essential to develop a comprehensive strategy in which all technologies capable of contributing to emissions reduction and system safety can be analysed and assessed methodically, transparently, and expertly. In addition to the energy and environmental dimensions, the measure also addresses economic and industrial development opportunities for our country.
"The Government recognises that a matter like nuclear energy arouses diverse opinions and sensitivities. For this very reason, it believes it is essential that public debate be based on accurate information, verifiable scientific data, and in-depth technical analysis. Transparency, participation, and dialogue with local communities are essential conditions for building a credible and shared path.
"The ultimate goal, fellow senators, remains to guarantee future generations a safe, sustainable, and competitive energy system capable of supporting Italy's economic and social development."
The bill
In October last year, Italy's Council of Ministers, at a meeting chaired by Meloni, approved a bill delegating responsibility for the reintroduction of nuclear energy in the country to the government. The bill empowers the government to comprehensively regulate the introduction of 'sustainable' nuclear power, within the framework of European policies for decarbonisation by 2050 and energy security objectives. The mandate includes, among other things, the development of a National Programme for Sustainable Nuclear Power, the establishment of an independent Nuclear Safety Authority, the strengthening of scientific and industrial research, the development of new skills, and the implementation of information and awareness campaigns.
In June the bill was passed by the Chamber of Deputies - the lower house of Italy's parliament - with 155 votes in favour, 86 against and eight abstentions.
What next?
Italy already has a number of initiatives under way relating to small modular reactors and advanced nuclear technologies.
On the same day as the vote was held, France's Nuward and its parent company EDF, plus Edison and Italian industrial partners Ansaldo and Maire, stressed their "common vision for the development of small modular reactors (SMRs) in Europe and their ambition to deploy a first reactor in Italy by 2035".
As reported by World Nuclear News, Nuward said last week that it aims to have a fleet of 10 of its SMRs across five European Union member countries, with initial construction beginning in 2030. In a post on LinkedIn on Wednesday, Nuward said: "Beyond the deployment of a first reactor, this momentum creates tangible opportunities for Italian industry to contribute to the development of the technology and become part of the value chain of the future European #SMR programme."
France-headquartered lead-cooled advanced modular reactor developer Newcleo also has considerable operations in Italy, including the first non-nuclear precursor prototype of its lead-cooled fast reactor. Last year it signed a memorandum of understanding with Italian cement association Federbeton to assess the potential for Newcleo’s technologies to work with the cement industry.
Italy's nuclear background
Italy operated a total of four nuclear power plants starting in the early 1960s but decided to phase out nuclear power in a referendum that followed the 1986 Chernobyl accident. It closed its last two operating plants, Caorso and Trino Vercellese, in 1990.
In late March 2011, following the Fukushima Daiichi accident, the Italian government approved a moratorium of at least one year on construction of nuclear power plants in the country, which had been looking to restart its long-abandoned nuclear programme. In a poll held in June of that year, 94% of voters rejected the construction of any new nuclear reactors in Italy.
Since then, Italian public opinion has become more favourable towards nuclear energy. A poll conducted in June 2021 showed that one-third of Italians were in favour of reconsidering the use of nuclear energy in the country.
In May 2023, the Italian Parliament approved a motion to urge the government to consider incorporating nuclear power into the country's energy mix. In September of that year, the first meeting was held of the National Platform for Sustainable Nuclear Power, set up by the government to define a time frame for the possible resumption of nuclear energy in Italy and identify opportunities for the country's industrial chain already operating in the sector.

There are more than 20 million packages needing to be transported each year, and IAEA Director General Rafael Mariano Grossi told the packed meeting that although there had been progress with the issue, it "continues to present challenges internationally. Denials and delays are subtle but extremely negative things that continue to happen" even with "companies in countries that are in favour of the transportation. So there is a problem in communication, which should not exist. I think it's high time we really tackle this issue in a concerted way, in a coherent way and try to solve it as much as we can".
Why the issue matters
Canadian Ambassador to Austria and Permanent Representative to the International Organisations in Vienna, Alison Grant, said: "Delayed shipment can mean delayed cancer treatment, postponed diagnostic scans, disrupted industrial operations, interrupted research activities … we need transport systems that recognise the importance of reliable access to radioactive material for all peaceful applications and we need better international cooperation."
King Lee, Head of Policy and Industry Engagement for World Nuclear Association - whose Programme Lead - Fuel Cycle, Allarakha Vora, has been involved in the working group - said that the industry was actively supporting, as needed, measures to tackle the issue. He stressed in particular the fundamental importance of transport throughout the nuclear fuel cycle, and praised the revival of the national focal point system (where each country has an identified expert point of contact to help resolve issues).
Peter Bryant, outgoing CEO of the World Nuclear Transport Institute, told the event: "When we talk about a shipment being unnecessarily delayed or denied, we need to think about what is at the other end of that journey - it could be a patient waiting for treatment, it could be an industrial facility needing to inspect a critical component, it could be technology helping to keep food safe or reduce food waste, or it could be material supporting the generation of low-carbon energy. We are not simply facilitating the transport of radioactive material. We are facilitating the benefits that the nuclear radioactive material provides to society."
The White Paper
The working group, which was established for a four year duration and is due to hold its final meeting later this year, finalised the White Paper in April, and it has now been published and shared with IAEA member states.
The paper says that the main causes of delays and denial of shipment are: perception and cultural factors; awareness gaps; regulatory complexity; lack of harmonisation and administrative gaps; insurance and economic barriers; and carrier and logistics issues.
The main consequences are listed as: negative impact on patient healthcare; increased costs and resource use; operational delays leading to safety or security risks; and regulatory non-compliance risks.
Its eight mitigation measures were set out during the meeting, as shown in these two photos:
(Image: WNN)

As shown on the left-hand side of the above photos, the meeting was given an indication of the most relevant stakeholder - member states, operators and industry and international organisations - for the various proposed mitigation measures.
What next?
At its final working group meeting in December, its members will "discuss and refine the governance framework to maintain collective oversight of facilitation, to continue addressing the denial of shipment issue, with shared ownership and responsibility for a sustainable approach".
The meeting was told that responsibility increasingly rests with member states - "the key actors driving the call for solutions to take decisive, harmonised and sustained actions. The issue cannot be entirely eliminated, but the impacts of denial of shipment can significantly be reduced, as per the proposals of the White Paper".
Grossi assured the meeting of the IAEA's continuing support.
The IAEA maintains a list of National Competent Authorities for the Safe Transport of Radioactive Material and also a list of the 75 National Focal Points appointed worldwide as of August 2026.

In October 2025, the Dutch cabinet submitted an amendment to the Nuclear Energy Act to the House of Representatives to enable the continued operation of Borssele. The 485 MWe (net) pressurised water reactor has been in operation since 1973 and accounts for about 3% of the Netherlands' total electricity generation. Under the current Nuclear Energy Act, the plant may remain in operation up to the end of 2033. An application for the continuation of operations will not be processed after that date. However, the government has requested it remain in operation until 2054, if this can be done safely. The government had earlier said it would consider acquiring a stake in the Borssele plant should a decision be made to extend its operation beyond 2033.
The proposed amendment - which removes the 2033 shut down date, meaning a permit application for an extension of the plant's operating life can now be submitted - was adopted by the House of Representatives (the lower house of the bicameral parliament) on 16 June this year. The Senate (the upper house) adopted the proposal on 22 September.
"The Senate's approval marks an important milestone in the process towards extending the operating life," said EPZ CEO Marco Muilenburg. "Now that this legal obstacle has been removed, we can proceed with preparations for the permit application. This allows us to demonstrate that the nuclear power plant will continue to contribute to the Dutch energy supply safely, reliably, and responsibly in the future."
At the request of the government, EPZ has been working for some time on preparations for a comprehensive safety evaluation to demonstrate that the Borssele plant can continue to produce electricity safely and reliably after 2033. It said intensive consultations are taking place with the Netherlands Nuclear Safety and Radiation Protection Authority (ANVS), the licensing authority and regulator of nuclear safety in the Netherlands. The assessment will be conducted based on international safety standards established by the International Atomic Energy Agency. Part of the process involves a thorough analysis of the technical condition of the plant and the options for implementing additional improvements to further enhance safety.
In addition to safety, EPZ is also investigating other important aspects related to a longer service life, such as the fuel cycle and the necessary investments for the coming decades.
EPZ says that the operating extension could be officially applied for "around the summer of 2027".
On 23 September - the day after the Senate approval - the government announced it had reached an agreement on acquiring the 70% stake in EPZ held by ZEH Energy. ZEH Energy is owned by the Province of Zeeland and Zeeland municipalities, which had previously indicated that they did not see a role for themselves as shareholders in the extension of the nuclear power plant's operating life.
The state will pay EUR115.7 million (USD131.3 million) for the shares. In addition, as a shareholder, the central government is making EUR119 million in capital available to safeguard the stability of the company, for example to cover ongoing costs.
The shares will be definitively transferred once Parliament and the current shareholders (the Province of Zeeland and municipalities) have approved the agreement. The remaining 30% of EPZ remains in the hands of German energy company RWE.
"Nuclear energy will play an important role in a diverse and stable energy supply in the Netherlands," said Jo-Annes de Bat, State Secretary for Climate and Green Growth. "Acquiring the shares is an important step to keep the nuclear power plant open longer in the long term. In doing so, we retain not only a stable energy source but also a great deal of nuclear expertise."
In December 2021, the Netherlands' then coalition government placed nuclear power at the heart of its climate and energy policy. In addition to keeping the Borssele plant in operation for longer, the government also called for the construction of new reactors. Based on preliminary plans, two new reactors will be completed around 2035 and each will have a capacity of 1,000-1,650 MWe. The two reactors would provide 9-13% of the country's electricity production in 2035. The cabinet announced in December 2022 that it saw Borssele as the most suitable location for the construction of the new reactors. Three other locations are also being considered for the reactors: the Tweede Maasvlakte near Rotterdam, Terneuzen in Zeeland and Eemshaven in Groningen.

Saskatchewan will determine which locations in northwest Saskatchewan allow for at least two large reactors to be licensed, constructed, and operated, and for southeast Saskatchewan what commercial, financing, and market conditions need to be satisfied to create a business case for a final investment decision. Crown Investments Corporation Minister Jeremy Harrison added: "Nuclear power will be a cornerstone of a reliable, affordable and secure electricity system in Saskatchewan. This plan gives SaskPower a clear path to meet growing demand and support the investment and industries that keep our province strong."
In October last year, the Government of Saskatchewan released the Saskatchewan First Energy Security Strategy and Supply Plan, setting out its vision and long-term strategy for electricity in the province. The plan saw the provincial government reiterate its commitments to nuclear power, as communicated in the provincial Growth Plan and the Interprovincial Strategic Plan on Small Modular Reactors. Specifically, it said the Government of Saskatchewan would continue to examine the feasibility of two SMR units near Estevan, and evaluate the feasibility of large reactors and/or advanced SMRs to meet industry demand for electricity and heat to identify if either can be economically deployed in Saskatchewan.

It announced in 2024 that it had identified two potential sites for SMR deployment, both in the Estevan area. It also signed a memorandum of understanding with Cameco and Westinghouse to explore technical and commercial pathways to deploy Westinghouse's reactor technology, including the advanced AP1000 reactor and AP300 SMR for long-term electricity supply planning.
Saskatchewan is home to the largest and highest-grade uranium mines in the world, but does not currently have any nuclear power reactors. It is working alongside the provinces of Ontario, New Brunswick and Alberta on the deployment of SMRs under a joint strategic plan released in 2022.

news.title: Four key issues when building nuclear in different countries, according to Rosatom

scraped_data.text:
Lion, pictured above, said that Rosatom currently has an international order portfolio of 45 nuclear power units in 10 countries, as well as having completed units in five countries since 2010.
She said that based on Rosatom's experience, in terms of meeting the demand for new nuclear, there were "four priority areas where action is particularly important".
The first area: Delivering nuclear projects on time and on budget
She said: "This is a well-known priority, and the industry is already making significant efforts in this area. I would like to emphasise one fundamental point here. The project schedule cannot be delivered by the vendor alone. It is a shared responsibility of the vendor, the customer, and the host country. A nuclear power plant is not a standard construction project. It is a complex national strategic infrastructure project that requires continuous supervision, multiple regulatory approvals, and in many cases, engagement with international institutions. In our experience, delays may arise not only from construction-related factors, but also from regulatory approvals, which may hold up the next project stage. This is in particular relevant to newcomer countries, where the national regulator and the proper nuclear regulatory framework may still be under development.
"For this reason, building national nuclear expertise is crucial. IAEA support, knowledge exchange with experienced nuclear countries and industrial players, and continuous dialogue between the customer and the vendor are essential."
The second priority: Industrial capacity and supply chain resilience
Lion said: "Every nuclear power plant project must be adapted to the specifics of a particular country. At the same time, standardisation and supply chain resilience become crucial. Rosatom now has to build about 20 nuclear units in parallel in different countries. Just 15 years ago, our production capacity allowed us to manufacture one set of key equipment for a nuclear power plant per year. We understood that this could become a bottleneck and limit our ability to respond to growing market demand. Today, Rosatom can manufacture three such equipment sets per year. Supply chain resilience becomes even more important when we think about SMRs (small modular reactors). Manufacturers across the entire value chain must be able to deliver high-quality equipment on schedule. This is fundamental to scaling nuclear energy. At the same time, the nuclear industry must cooperate with … local construction companies, general equipment manufacturers, and other businesses involved in the development of infrastructure at the site."
She said that on average, about 100 companies are involved in Rosatom's overseas nuclear construction projects. "Localisation is an important factor in the successful delivery of the project and creates a boost for economic growth in the region. According to our estimates, the multiplier effect on related sectors of the economy of the region may reach ten times the total investment into the project itself," she added.
The third priority: Workforce
"Nuclear professions require a highly specialised knowledge base. Not every country has academic infrastructure to train nuclear engineers and operators at scale. These are long-term, high-skill jobs guaranteed for decades, and the key challenge for the industry is to ensure that we have a sufficient amount of professionals to build and operate the nuclear power plant," she said.
"There is no universal model here. In many cases, key specialists involved in the implementation of our nuclear power projects abroad have to come from Russia. And given that nuclear construction projects last for many years, they often move with their families. This means that the project company must also address broader social infrastructure needs, including decent living conditions and access to education for employees' children," added Lion.
"This may seem like a practical detail, but in reality, this is an important component of the nuclear power plant project's sustainability. For example, during the implementation of the Akkuyu Nuclear Power Plant in Turkey, new residential villages were developed with Rosatom support. A new school was opened there, attended by the children of Akkuyu Power Plant employees and by children from local communities. In other cases, experienced personnel may move from one international project to another. For example, from Belarus to Egypt or from Egypt to Bangladesh. This rotation helps transfer practical knowledge and skills across projects and maintain level of qualification among employees.
"At the same time, the long-term objective is to develop qualified personnel within the host country. The full training cycle for a nuclear engineer takes around six years. If we are serious about tripling nuclear capacity in the coming decades, we must make careers in nuclear more visible, more attractive, and more relevant for the next generation of professionals. Public communication, bloggers, podcasts, role models, and success stories can all help us to achieve this."
The fourth priority: Financing
"Access to finance has always been one of the industry's most complex challenges, In this regard, Rosatom has been in a relatively strong position as many of our international projects have been supported by intergovernmental loans, but this model is not universal. Over recent years the global nuclear community, with important leadership from World Nuclear Association and the IAEA, have done significant work to build dialogue with the international financial community. The global green agenda has also played an important role, and the contribution of nuclear energy to climate goals and to sustainable development is well recognised today. We've learned how to issue green bonds and use ESG-linked financing instruments.
"Last year, we saw breakthrough announcements. The World Bank, followed by the New Development Bank and the Asian Development Bank, and many others expressed clear interest in supporting nuclear energy projects. The key task for the nuclear community now is to convert this interest into bankable nuclear power plant projects and particular transactions. Based on our experience, banks are more interested in discussing SMR projects - they require shorter construction timelines and significantly lower capital investment compared with large scale nuclear power plants. We are also seeing growing investment interest in nuclear projects from end users who want to secure access to low-carbon energy.
"At the same time, we should remember that nuclear energy is still relatively new and not a fully familiar asset class for the financial market. This is why dialogue remains crucial - the more nuclear professionals, policy makers, financial organisations, universities, and climate experts talk to each other, the faster we will find practical solutions for tripling nuclear capacity."
She concluded by saying that Rosatom's experience "confirms that global nuclear ambitions cannot be achieved without partnership, mutual trust, and open dialogue".
World Nuclear Symposium, organised by World Nuclear Association, took place in London from 9-11 September.

Subsequent units would be implemented every 2-3 years. The coastal towns of Lubiatowo and Kopalino in Poland's Choczewo municipality in the province of Pomerania were named as the preferred location for the country's first large nuclear power plant.
In November 2022, the Polish government announced the first plant, with a capacity of 3,750 MWe, would be built in Pomerania using Westinghouse's AP1000 technology. The updated programme includes the construction of two nuclear power plants with a total capacity of up to 9 GWe, human resources and infrastructure development, increasing the participation of domestic industry, and strengthening the nuclear regulatory system. The adopted document outlines timelines for the construction of the first and second nuclear power plants, as well as key assumptions for the implementation of the second plant.
"The update of the PPEJ takes into account the changes that have affected the European energy market in recent years - from the energy crisis and Russia's aggression against Ukraine to the growing demand of industry for predictable and low-emission energy," the Ministry of Energy said.
The ministry said the update provides increased funding for tasks related to the implementation of nuclear energy: support for building competencies in the field of nuclear energy, support for the participation of Polish industry in the Polish Nuclear Power Programme, and strengthening the nuclear regulatory institution, that is, the National Atomic Energy Agency (NAEA). It noted support for the NAEA constitutes the largest financial component of the Polish Nuclear Power Programme, which is particularly important as it will contribute to increasing the effectiveness and efficiency of the licensing process and ensuring an adequate level of national nuclear safety and radiological protection for Polish citizens.
Revised timeline
For the project to construct the first plant - for which preparatory work at the construction site and the implementation of accompanying infrastructure is under way - PLN60.2 billion (USD15.4 billion) has been allocated for the project's recapitalisation between 2025 and 2030. The financing model assumes a combination of equity and debt financing supported by domestic and international institutions.

Priority areas

"It is estimated that Polish companies could contribute approximately 40% of the project's value during the construction of the first reactor. With the development of subsequent units, as expertise, experience, and the number of certified companies grow, this share could rise to approximately 70%."
The update to the programme indicates key areas of state action to ensure effective implementation of the programme: development of staff and competences for the nuclear sector; development of transmission infrastructure; increasing the share of domestic industry; strengthening the nuclear and technical supervision system; radioactive waste management; and communication and social education.

According to the developers, under large-radius operating conditions in nuclear power plants, its lifting capacity is about 50% higher than that of similar foreign products, and it can meet the relevant hoisting operation requirements at a single station and under a single operating condition.
In terms of operation, the equipment adopts a fully electric drive mode and can be directly connected to 10kV industrial mains power, featuring zero emissions and low noise. The crane - jointly developed by Sany Heavy Machinery and China Energy Engineering Guangdong Thermal Power Special Equipment Co Ltd - was produced at Sany's Huzhou Industrial Park in Zhejiang.
This crane was developed to meet the construction needs of the Hualong One 2.0 nuclear power plant's "one machine, two islands" system - this is where one ring-rail crane is positioned between two nuclear islands, allowing for the lifting of all modules and main equipment of both units with a single positioning and boom length.
"This marks a key breakthrough in the localisation of ultra-large tonnage nuclear power plant lifting equipment in China," China General Nuclear (CGN) said. The contract covers engineering and design services, project delivery, as well as programme and project management associated with the CANDU reactors, including work that would enable Unit 5 to operate until the 2060s, AtkinsRéalis said. "Advancing the Pickering Nuclear Refurbishment Project is another significant milestone in Ontario's clean energy future and further demonstrates the strength of Aecon's comprehensive nuclear construction expertise," Aecon Group President and CEO Jean-Louis Servranckx said. "Building on decades of experience successfully delivering the largest and most complex nuclear projects across North America, our teams are proud to support OPG in extending the life of this important nuclear generating station while helping ensure a reliable supply of low-carbon electricity for Ontario."
"AtkinsRéalis brings decades of hands-on experience refurbishing Canadian-owned CANDU reactors in Ontario, with a proven track record of delivering complex life-extension work safely, reliably and with the discipline required for on-time and on-budget performance," AtkinsRéalis President and CEO Ian Edwards said. "This work at the Pickering station will help ensure Ontario continues to benefit from reliable, affordable and low-carbon electricity for decades to come."
Pickering units 5-8 began operations in the mid-1980s and had been scheduled to end electricity production this year, but in 2022 the provincial government directed OPG to keep them in operation until 2026 and to reassess the feasibility of refurbishing the units. President and CEO Nicolle Butcher said that since the first unit at Pickering A began operating in 1971, the plant has established itself as one of the world's largest and best-performing nuclear facilities. The last of the Pickering A units, Pickering unit 4, was permanently shut down at the end of 2024.
"When the previous government planned to shut down Pickering, our government chose to protect 4,500 jobs and create 30,500 new jobs by doubling down on Canadian workers, technology and energy sovereignty," Stephen Lecce, Ontario's Minister of Energy and Mines, said.
